blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html:
A life table follows a hypothetical group of 100,000 births (the radix) through the age-specific death rates of one period, recording at each age how many survive and how many years they will live. Its columns are:

  • ₙMₓ: death rate between ages x and x + n (deaths ÷ mid-year population);
  • ₙqₓ: probability that a person alive at exact age x dies before x + n;
  • lₓ: number alive at exact age x;
  • ₙdₓ = lₓ × ₙqₓ: deaths between x and x + n;
  • ₙLₓ: person-years lived between x and x + n;
  • Tₓ: total person-years lived beyond age x;
  • eₓ = Tₓ/lₓ: life expectancy at age x, the average number of further years lived by those who reach x.

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html: A life table turns a set of age-specific death rates into survival. Imagine 100,000 babies who experience, at each age, the death rates observed this year. Count how many die in each age band, how many years everyone lives in total, and divide by the number starting out. The result, e₀, summarises a whole mortality pattern in one number that does not depend on the population’s age structure. This is a current (period) life table. A cohort life table instead follows people actually born in one year until all have died. An abridged table uses age bands, as here; a complete table uses single years.

blocks.label: Derivation
blocks.html:
From rate to probability. In a band of width n, let aₓ be the average years lived in the band by those who die in it. Person-years lived in the band are ₙLₓ = n(lₓ − ₙdₓ) + aₓ × ₙdₓ, and the death rate is ₙMₓ = ₙdₓ/ₙLₓ. Substitute ₙdₓ = lₓ × q and ₙLₓ = lₓ[n − (n − aₓ)q], then solve for q:

ₙqₓ = n × ₙMₓ/[1 + (n − aₓ) × ₙMₓ].

Survivors. Surviving each band is conditional on reaching it (recall §5.3), so lₓ₊ₙ = lₓ × (1 − ₙqₓ).

Open last band (60+). Everyone dies, so q = 1 and d = l. With a constant death rate M, person-years = l/M, so e₆₀ = 1/M₆₀.

Life expectancy. Tₓ = sum of ₙLₓ from age x upwards; eₓ = Tₓ/lₓ.

blocks.label: Worked Calculation
blocks.html:
data/lifetable_district.csv gives mid-year population and deaths in seven age bands for a hypothetical Chhattisgarh district. For this example, a = 0.1 year for infants who die (reflecting deaths concentrated in the first weeks of life), 1.6 years for ages 1–4, and n/2 for other bands; these values are assumptions of the example.

Age x n ₙMₓ ₙqₓ lₓ ₙdₓ ₙLₓ Tₓ eₓ
0 1 0.0310 0.0302 100,000 3,016 97,286 6,774,296 67.7
1 4 0.0024 0.0095 96,984 926 385,715 6,677,010 68.8
5 10 0.0007 0.0070 96,058 670 957,234 6,291,295 65.5
15 15 0.0015 0.0222 95,388 2,122 1,414,908 5,334,061 55.9
30 15 0.0030 0.0440 93,266 4,105 1,368,205 3,919,154 42.0
45 15 0.0090 0.1265 89,161 11,276 1,252,853 2,550,948 28.6
60+ — 0.0600 1.0000 77,886 77,886 1,298,095 1,298,095 16.7
  1. Age 0: M = 93/3,000 = 0.0310. q₀ = 0.0310/(1 + 0.9 × 0.0310) = 0.0302. So 1,000 × q₀ = 30.2 infant deaths per 1,000 live births, the life-table form of the IMR.
  2. d₀ = 100,000 × 0.0302 = 3,016; l₁ = 96,984.
  3. L₀ = 1 × (100,000 − 3,016) + 0.1 × 3,016 = 97,286 person-years.
  4. Ages 1–4: M = 30/12,500 = 0.0024; q = 4 × 0.0024/(1 + 2.4 × 0.0024) = 0.0095; d = 926; L = 4 × (96,984 − 926) + 1.6 × 926 = 385,715.
  5. Continue down the table. At 60+: q = 1, L₆₀ = 77,886/0.06 = 1,298,095, and e₆₀ = 1/0.06 = 16.7 years.
  6. T₀ = sum of all L = 6,774,296. e₀ = 6,774,296/100,000 = 67.7 years.
  7. e₁ = 6,677,010/96,984 = 68.8 years, more than e₀, because a baby who survives the high-risk first year has left that risk behind.
  8. Probability of surviving from birth to 60 = l₆₀/l₀ = 77,886/100,000 = 0.779.

blocks.alt: Survivorship curve from the abridged life table
blocks.caption: Figure 7.4. Survivors lₓ out of 100,000 births. The steep drop in the first year and after age 45 shows where deaths concentrate. The curve stops at 60 because the last band is open.

blocks.label: In R (optional)
blocks.html:
lt <- read.csv("data/lifetable_district.csv")
n  <- c(1, 4, 10, 15, 15, 15, NA)           # interval widths
a  <- c(0.1, 1.6, 5, 7.5, 7.5, 7.5, NA)     # years lived if dying
M  <- lt$deaths / lt$midyear_pop             # nMx
q  <- n * M / (1 + (n - a) * M); q[7] <- 1   # nqx
l  <- 100000 * cumprod(c(1, 1 - q[-7]))      # lx
d  <- l * q                                  # ndx
L  <- n * (l - d) + a * d; L[7] <- l[7] / M[7]   # nLx
Tx <- rev(cumsum(rev(L)))                    # Tx
e  <- Tx / l                                 # ex
data.frame(age = lt$age_start, M = round(M, 4), q = round(q, 4),
           l = round(l), d = round(d), L = round(L), T = round(Tx),
           e = round(e, 1))
  age      M      q      l     d       L       T    e
1   0 0.0310 0.0302 100000  3016   97286 6774296 67.7
2   1 0.0024 0.0095  96984   926  385715 6677010 68.8
3   5 0.0007 0.0070  96058   670  957234 6291295 65.5
4  15 0.0015 0.0222  95388  2122 1414908 5334061 55.9
5  30 0.0030 0.0440  93266  4105 1368205 3919154 42.0
6  45 0.0090 0.1265  89161 11276 1252853 2550948 28.6
7  60 0.0600 1.0000  77886 77886 1298095 1298095 16.7

Each line of code is one column of the table: the rate-to-probability conversion, the cumulative product that builds lₓ, the person-years, the reverse cumulative sum that builds Tₓ, and eₓ. The printed rows reproduce the hand-worked table.

points.html: e₀ is not “the age at which people die”. It is the mean of the life-table distribution of ages at death. High infant mortality pulls e₀ down, which is why e₁ can exceed e₀.
Period tables are snapshots. e₀ = 67.7 is what a baby would live if this year’s death rates held for life. Falling mortality means real cohorts usually live longer.

The IMR as a probability. WHO defines the IMR as the life-table probability of dying before age 1 (WHO IMR metadata). Here 1,000 × q₀ = 30.2, close to, but not the same as, the death rate at age 0 (1,000 × M₀ = 31.0).
Choices of aₓ matter for infants. When infant deaths cluster early in life, a₀ is well below 0.5, and the value chosen changes q₀ and e₀. State the values you assume.

Link to survival analysis. The life table’s lₓ/l₀ is a survival curve built from grouped population data. §14.4 (Kaplan–Meier, the survival curve estimated from individuals’ follow-up times) builds the same curve from a cohort in which people are followed for different lengths of time.

questions.prompt: In a 5-year band, the death rate is 0.02 per person-year and those who die live on average 2.5 years in the band. Compute ₅qₓ.
Using the table above, what is the probability that a 15-year-old survives to age 45?
If the open 60+ band had a death rate of 0.05 per person-year, what would e₆₀ be? Why can e₁ exceed e₀?
questions.answer: e₆₀ = 1/M = 1/0.05 = 20 years. e₁ can exceed e₀ because e₀ averages over everyone born, including the many who die in infancy; a child who survives the first year has passed that high-risk period, so its expected remaining life can be longer than a newborn’s (here 68.8 vs 67.7 years).
